clinicalPearls: ARDS is a clinical syndrome of severe dyspnea of rapid onset, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure, caused by diffuse lung injury (Harrison 22e p.2299).

By 2012 expert consensus, ARDS is graded as mild, moderate, or severe by the degree of hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), and these stages correlate with mortality risk and duration of mechanical ventilation in survivors (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).

Most cases (>80%) arise from a small number of disorders: pneumonia and sepsis (~40-60%), followed by aspiration of gastric contents, trauma, multiple transfusions, and drug overdose; risk rises with more than one predisposing condition (Harrison 22e p.2299).
The natural history has three phases - exudative (first ~7 days), proliferative (~day 7-21), and fibrotic - each with characteristic clinical and pathologic features (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2301).

Cornerstone of management is recognizing and treating the underlying trigger (pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma) plus standardized bundled ICU care, rather than ARDS-specific drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2302).

Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and limited plateau pressure (<=30 cmH2O) significantly lowers mortality versus conventional higher tidal volumes; this is the only therapy graded by the strongest evidence (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303).

Prone positioning early in severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) reduced 28-day mortality in a randomized trial; it requires a team experienced in proning because repositioning critically ill patients can be hazardous (Harrison 22e p.2302).

A conservative fluid strategy - reducing left atrial filling pressure with fluid restriction and diuretics - shortens ICU stay and duration of ventilation, limited only by hypotension and organ hypoperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2302).
Mortality in ARDS is largely due to nonpulmonary causes, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure accounting for >80% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2303).
harrison.pathophysiology: ARDS results from diffuse lung injury, either direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, toxic inhalation, pulmonary contusion) or indirect (e.g., sepsis, severe trauma, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis). It evolves through three phases. In the EXUDATIVE phase (first ~7 days), alveolar capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes are injured, the tight alveolar barrier is lost, and protein-rich edema fluid accumulates in the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and lipid mediators recruit neutrophils, and condensed plasma proteins plus cellular debris and dysfunctional surfactant form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). Pulmonary vascular injury occurs early with microthrombi. Dependent alveolar collapse reduces lung compliance, producing intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and increased work of breathing; microvascular occlusion raises dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance, so hypercapnia and pulmonary hypertension can also occur. The PROLIFERATIVE phase (~day 7-21) brings lung repair, organization of exudates, a shift from neutrophil- to lymphocyte-predominant infiltrates, and proliferation of type II pneumocytes that regenerate surfactant and differentiate into type I cells; most patients recover. Some progress to the FIBROTIC phase, with alveolar-duct and interstitial fibrosis, emphysema-like bullae, vascular occlusion and pulmonary hypertension, increased pneumothorax risk, reduced compliance, and increased dead space (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300, p.2301, p.2302).
additionalDifferentials: Acute interstitial lung disease (e.g., acute interstitial pneumonitis)
infectionMimics: Bilateral pneumonia (may also coexist with ARDS)
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas to determine PaO2/FiO2 ratio for Berlin severity grading
Chest radiograph (bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, often involving >=three-quarters of lung fields)
Echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic/cardiac etiology when no ARDS risk factor is present
Chest CT (shows bilateral infiltrates with heterogeneous, often dependent lung involvement)
Lung ultrasound permitted as an alternative imaging modality under proposed 2023 Berlin updates, especially in resource-limited settings
redFlags: Progressive hypoxemia and increasing work of breathing leading to respiratory fatigue and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg) carrying the highest mortality
Concurrent sepsis or multiorgan failure, which account for most ARDS deaths
Lung biopsy evidence of pulmonary fibrosis in any phase, associated with increased mortality
harrison.prognosis: Hospital mortality in the LUNG SAFE study was approximately 34.9% for mild, 40.3% for moderate, and 46.1% for severe ARDS, with a trend toward improved outcomes over time. Increasing Berlin-defined severity predicts higher mortality. Most deaths are nonpulmonary, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure causing >80%. Major mortality risk factors are nonpulmonary: advanced age (~60% mortality in patients >75 vs ~20% in those <45), preexisting organ dysfunction (chronic liver disease, chronic alcohol abuse, chronic immunosuppression); direct lung injury carries nearly twice the death risk of indirect injury. Among survivors, the lung has notable resolving power: most regain nearly normal lung function, usually within 6 months, and more than a third have normal spirometry and diffusion capacity one year after extubation. However, exercise limitation and reduced physical quality of life are often documented at 5 years despite near-normal pulmonary function, and survivors and family caregivers carry a substantial burden of depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (Harrison 22e p.2303, p.2304).
pitfalls: ARDS radiographic findings are characteristic but not specific and can be indistinguishable from cardiogenic pulmonary edema; unlike cardiogenic edema, ARDS often lacks cardiomegaly, pleural effusions, or pulmonary vascular redistribution. Hydrostatic edema must not be the primary cause - if no ARDS risk factor is present, objective evaluation (e.g., echocardiography) is required to exclude a cardiac etiology (Harrison 22e p.2300, p.2301).

Mechanical ventilation, though life-saving, can aggravate lung injury via volutrauma (alveolar overdistention from excess tidal volume), barotrauma (high alveolar pressure), and atelectrauma (recurrent alveolar collapse); because ARDS lung is heterogeneous, fully inflating consolidated regions can overdistend and injure more normal lung (Harrison 22e p.2302).

Routine glucocorticoids are NOT supported by current evidence for ARDS itself; recruitment maneuvers combined with higher baseline PEEP increased mortality in one study; routine early neuromuscular blockade is not beneficial in all moderate-to-severe ARDS (reserve for ventilatory dyssynchrony despite sedation); surfactant replacement and inhaled vasodilators (e.g., inhaled nitric oxide) do not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303).
Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, so correlation with PaO2 should be considered when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2300).
harrison.severityClassification: Berlin definition (2012): severity is graded by oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 assessed on at least 5 cmH2O PEEP) - Mild: 200 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=300 mmHg; Moderate: 100 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=200 mmHg; Severe: PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg. Onset must be acute (within 1 week of a clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms), chest imaging must show bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure must not be primarily due to hydrostatic (cardiogenic) edema (objective evaluation such as echocardiography required if no ARDS risk factor present). Proposed 2023 updates extend criteria to nonintubated patients on high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, add SpO2/FiO2 (S/F) ratios, permit ultrasound imaging, and allow application in resource-limited settings. A more recent global definition has also been proposed that does not rely on arterial blood gases, chest radiography, or PEEP (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).
